chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the man who is prone to doubt in his prayer, so he doubts about the bowing and does not know if he bowed or not, and he doubts about the prostration and does not know if he prostrated or not, he said: 'He does not prostrate and does not bow, but continues in his prayer until he is certain with certainty.'

And regarding the man who forgets a prostration and remembers it after he stood up and bowed, he said: 'He continues in his prayer and does not prostrate until he gives the salutation (taslim); when he gives the salutation, he prostrates for what he missed.' I said: 'And if he does not remember except after that (i.e., after the final taslim)?' He said: 'He makes up what he missed when he remembers it.'

And this ruling regarding forgetting the prostration applies specifically to the last two rak'ahs, because for the first two rak'ahs, if he doubts regarding the prostration in them, he repeats; what indicates this is what he narrated.

key_terms.الرَّكْعَتَانِ الْآخِرَتَانِ: The last two rak'ahs of the prayer
key_terms.الْوَهْمُ: Excessive doubt or hesitation in religious acts
key_terms.يَقْضِي: To make up (a missed ritual act)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a person who frequently doubts whether they performed bowing or prostration during prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between *wahm* (minor doubt) and *shakk* (major doubt), establishing that minor uncertainty does not invalidate the prayer but requires the worshipper to proceed with certainty. It further details the specific protocol for *sujud al-sahw* (prostration of forgetfulness), noting that if one forgets a prostration and remembers after completing the final sitting, they must perform the missed prostration after the final salam, a ruling particularly emphasized for the last two rak'ahs. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on ease and the preservation of prayer validity amidst common human error.
